Volume 06 · Chapter 09

Fiscal policy and public debt

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v06-c08

By the endDerive debt dynamics and evaluate fiscal trade-offs with explicit assumptions.

Capability and prerequisites

After this chapter, you can reconcile a government's debt stock with its budget and financing flows, derive exact debt-to-GDP dynamics, test a proposed fiscal rule, and compare stabilization and distributional effects under explicit assumptions. You can explain why a primary deficit, a cash shortage, and an unsustainable fiscal path are different diagnoses.

Read Business cycles and stabilization, retaining the accounts in Chapter 1, dated household budgets in Chapter 4, and balance sheets in Chapter 6. We use geometric sequences, present values and linear equations. All numerical economies, policy parameters and problems below are original synthetic experiments. They are not observations, forecasts or recommendations for an actual government.

1. Start with the government boundary and the dates

A government can collect more taxes than it spends on current programs and still borrow: it may owe interest, replace maturing bonds or acquire financial assets. Conversely, selling an asset can reduce borrowing without improving the recurring tax–spending balance. A debt ratio alone does not reveal these transactions.

Fix the institutional perimeter, currency, valuation convention and period. Our baseline is a single consolidated government issuing domestic-currency debt at par, with no default, indexation or currency revaluation. Bₜ is the nominal principal outstanding at the end of period t; iₜ is the ordinary net interest rate paid during t on Bₜ₋₁; Rₜ = 1 + iₜ > 0. Thus the interest subscript records the payment period. It is not the rate paid on newly issued end-t debt. Initial B₀ is given.

Let Tₜ denote revenue and Hₜ noninterest spending. H includes government consumption, public investment and transfers. Define the nominal primary surplus Sₜ = Tₜ − Hₜ: a primary deficit makes S negative. This fiscal spending aggregate is broader than the G for government consumption in the expenditure identity Y = C + I + G + NX; public investment belongs in I there and transfers are not purchases of current output. Consistent definitions prevent counting either twice.

Bₜ − Bₜ₋₁ = iₜBₜ₋₁ − Sₜ + Aₜ,
Bₜ = RₜBₜ₋₁ − Sₜ + Aₜ.

Aₜ is an explicitly reconciled stock–flow adjustment: debt changes beyond interest minus the primary surplus. In our cash examples it is net acquisition of financial assets, including cash accumulation; drawing down cash makes it negative. In broader accounts it can also include valuation, coverage and timing adjustments. Every application must list its components instead of using A as an unexplained balancing item. In the simple model, the overall deficit before these adjustments is iB − S.

Suppose a government pays 15 for a financial claim worth only 5 at the transaction date. Calling the whole payment an asset worth 15 conceals a loss or transfer. A transparent decomposition records an asset of 5 and a transfer/loss component of 10 under the stated accounting treatment; together they still require 15 of cash. If the claim instead pays 5 at a later date, discount it before making this comparison. Actual statistical classification depends on the instrument and valuation convention. Never record the full 15 as primary expense and then add the same full 15 again as financial acquisition.

Gross debt measures specified liabilities. A chosen net-debt measure deducts specified financial assets on a comparable basis; which assets qualify must be stated. A hospital is useful public capital, but it is not automatically cash available to redeem a bond tomorrow. Consolidating a Treasury with its central bank removes their claims on one another, while retaining liabilities to the private sector. It does not erase the economy's resource constraints.

If Mₜ principal matures during t, all financing is at par, and Aₜ consists only of financing cash flows, gross new issuance is

Qₜ = Mₜ + iₜBₜ₋₁ − Sₜ + Aₜ,
Bₜ = Bₜ₋₁ − Mₜ + Qₜ.

Replacing maturing principal is refinancing, not an additional deficit. The maturity schedule determines how much funding must be raised now even when the ending stock is unchanged. This equation assumes Q ≥ 0 and enough market access; a negative value calls for an explicit debt-buyback or asset-accumulation rule. With noncash valuation changes in A, strip those out of the cash financing equation. A portfolio with several coupons uses the actual interest bill in place of iB; i can summarize that bill as an effective rate when B > 0.

2. Exact real and GDP-scaled debt dynamics

Let Pₜ > 0 be the GDP deflator, Yₜ > 0 real GDP and Zₜ = PₜYₜ nominal GDP. Ordinary inflation is πₜ = Pₜ/Pₜ₋₁ − 1 and real growth is gₜ = Yₜ/Yₜ₋₁ − 1, both greater than −1. These are ordinary fractional rates, unlike the log-point equations in Chapter 8. Nominal GDP grows by the exact factor Γₜ = (1 + πₜ)(1 + gₜ). Divide the nominal budget by current prices:

Dₜ = [Rₜ/(1 + πₜ)]Dₜ₋₁ − Sₜ/Pₜ + Aₜ/Pₜ,   Dₜ = Bₜ/Pₜ.

The realized real gross carrying factor is Rₜ/(1 + πₜ). Inflation reduces the purchasing power of a fixed inherited nominal promise; it need not reduce the cost of indexed debt, foreign-currency debt or new borrowing after investors revise rates. No permanent fiscal resource follows merely from renaming nominal liabilities.

Define dₜ = Bₜ/Zₜ, pₜ = Sₜ/Zₜ and aₜ = Aₜ/Zₜ. Both fiscal flows use current GDP, while inherited debt uses prior GDP. The exact law is

dₜ = αₜdₜ₋₁ − pₜ + aₜ,   αₜ = Rₜ/Γₜ,
Δdₜ = [(iₜ − πₜ − gₜ − πₜgₜ)/((1 + πₜ)(1 + gₜ))]dₜ₋₁ − pₜ + aₜ.

Alternatively define 1 + rₜ = Rₜ/(1 + πₜ). Then αₜ = (1 + rₜ)/(1 + gₜ), so Δd = [(r − g)/(1 + g)]dₜ₋₁ − p + a. The familiar (r − g)d − p expression is a first-order approximation, not the exact identity. Multiplying a percent rate written as 5 rather than 0.05 by a fractional debt ratio introduces another factor-of-100 error.

Escolano's debt-dynamics note supplies the scoped methodological reference for exact GDP scaling and the distinction between a stationary ratio and a stable adjustment path. Its basic equations abstract from several nonbudget debt changes; our A ledger makes those changes explicit. We derive our numerical cases independently and do not import its historical rate estimates.

Worked example 1 — A small stock change and a large financing operation

Opening debt is B₀ = 120 and nominal GDP is Z₀ = 200. Let i₁ = 0.04, π₁ = 0.02 and g₁ = 1/34. Then Γ₁ = 1.05 and Z₁ = 210. The primary surplus is 4.2, exactly 2% of current GDP. The government also acquires a liquid financial asset at its fair value of 6, funded by debt: A₁ = 6.

Interest is 4.8; the overall deficit before acquisition is 4.8 − 4.2 = 0.6. Ending debt is 124.8 − 4.2 + 6 = 126.6. Gross debt increases by 6.6, and its ratio rises from 0.6 to 126.6/210 = 211/350 ≈ 0.602857. Directly, α = 104/105, p = 1/50 and a = 1/35 produce the same answer. Although nominal GDP growth exceeds the effective interest rate, acquisition raises gross debt enough to increase this period's ratio.

If only 60 of principal matures, new issuance is 60 + 4.8 − 4.2 + 6 = 66.6. The stock identity gives 120 − 60 + 66.6 = 126.6. If all 120 matures instead, issuance is 126.6; the ending stock is identical, but the funding need is much larger. Neither issuance figure is the deficit.

With no opening financial asset and the acquired asset valued at 6, the specified net debt ends at 120.6. Its ratio is 201/350 ≈ 0.574286, below the opening 0.6. This does not prove the acquisition was wise: that requires its risk, return and purpose. It shows why gross and net measures can move differently. Liquidity also depends on whether the asset can actually be sold at the recorded value when needed.

3. Stationary debt, stability and feasible fiscal responses

Set a = 0 and hold α > 0 and p constant. Repeated substitution gives dₜ = αᵗd₀ − p∑ⱼ₌₀ᵗ⁻¹αʲ. For α ≠ 1, define d* = p/(α − 1); then

dₜ = d* + αᵗ(d₀ − d*).

If 0 < α < 1, deviations shrink. A positive stationary debt ratio in this case requires a primary deficit, p < 0. A constant positive surplus ultimately implies net asset accumulation in the algebra; it cannot be reported as negative gross debt. If α > 1, a positive p permits a positive d*, but deviations grow: above the fixed point, debt rises; below it, debt falls and can reach zero. Maintaining the surplus consistent with one exact ratio is not a rule that attracts nearby ratios. If α = 1, the separate formula is dₜ = d₀ − tp. A stationary ratio then requires p = 0, and a nonzero initial deviation persists.

To target d̄, suppose fiscal policy can implement pₜ = p̄ + φ(dₜ₋₁ − d̄), where p̄ = (α − 1)d̄. Substitution yields dₜ − d̄ = (α − φ)(dₜ₋₁ − d̄). The target is asymptotically stable exactly when |α − φ| < 1 in this linear model. Equality gives persistence or alternating deviations; a larger absolute value amplifies them. This mathematical condition says nothing by itself about whether the required taxes or spending cuts are feasible or desirable.

Worked example 2 — The surplus that holds a target need not restore it

Take Γ = 1.02, R = 1.071, hence α = 1.05. Target d̄ = 0.8 requires p̄ = 0.04. If policy fixes p at 0.04 and actual initial debt is 0.9, the next three ratios are 0.905, 0.91025 and 0.9157625. If initial debt is 0.7, the corresponding third ratio is 0.6842375. Both move away from the target.

Now use φ = 0.25 with no binding fiscal cap. The deviation factor is 0.8. Starting at 0.9 gives debt ratios 0.88, 0.864 and 0.8512, with primary-surplus ratios 0.065, 0.06 and 0.056. The rule restores the target by demanding larger surpluses when debt is above it. Starting from 0.9, the first surplus is 6.5% of current GDP; it must not be described as feasible merely because the equation can be evaluated.

A stronger response need not converge. With φ = 2.1 the factor is −1.05: the first deviation changes from +0.1 to −0.105 and the next to +0.11025. The oscillations grow. Eventually they also violate a nonnegative gross-debt domain, at which point the model must stop or specify an asset regime. The criterion is about the whole feedback system, not the size of φ in isolation.

A useful conditional debt-capacity calculation assumes α > 1 is permanently fixed and the primary-surplus ratio can never exceed pmax. If d > pmax/(α − 1), even the maximum surplus makes next-period debt grow. Repeating that maximum yields an explosive positive deviation from this threshold. If d is below it, the maximum surplus lowers debt under these assumptions. The equality case holds the ratio constant. This is an arithmetic bound inside a deterministic model, not a universal safe debt level: growth, borrowing rates, revenue capacity, political feasibility, assets, maturity and contingent liabilities can all change it.

For time-varying rates, multiply the actual α factors and carry forward each dated fiscal flow; do not replace them with an unqualified average. With uncertainty, E[R/Γ] generally differs from E[R]/E[Γ]. A stress scenario is a conditional path, not a probability forecast unless the probabilities and estimation method have been supplied.

4. The present-value constraint and the funding calendar

For a clean intertemporal argument return to one-period nominal debt with A = 0 and Rₜ > 0. Divide each budget equation by DtR = ∏ⱼ₌₁ᵗRⱼ, where D0R = 1. This discount-factor denominator is separate from the real-debt symbol D above. Summing cancels intermediate discounted debt stocks:

B₀ = ∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ Sₜ/DtR + BT/DTR.

This finite identity follows from the period budgets; it does not authorize dropping the terminal term. A finite model may require BT = 0. An infinite model may impose the stronger vanishing discounted terminal-debt condition lim BT/DTR = 0; under that condition the present value of primary surpluses equals B₀. It is an explicit financing/terminal restriction, not an algebraic consequence of issuing a bond. If the government owns assets, carries guarantees or changes its financing instruments, include their cash flows and terminal values consistently before applying a solvency test.

For constant R > 1 and a constant nominal primary surplus S, the infinite present value is S/(R − 1). This uses a constant currency amount, not a constant share of growing GDP. A bounded debt ratio is a different condition. For example, let R = 1.02, Γ = 1.05 and dₜ = 0.8 forever. Then α = 34/35 and p = (α − 1)0.8 = −4/175: a primary deficit of about 2.286% of current GDP holds the ratio constant. Yet Bₜ/Rᵗ = 0.8Z₀(1.05/1.02)ᵗ grows, violating the imposed vanishing-terminal condition.

The counterexample demonstrates that these two tests are not interchangeable. It does not prove that every economy with growth above interest is infeasible. Models in which debt supplies liquidity or transfers resources across generations can have different equilibrium and terminal conditions. State those conditions before asserting a policy opportunity or impossibility. Conversely, a present-value resource calculation does not establish that investors will refinance debt at the required date and rate.

Fiscal space is the capacity to undertake a useful fiscal action under acceptable financing, repayment and macroeconomic risks. An operational assessment asks what is due when; what currency and interest exposures exist; what revenues, spending adjustments and saleable assets are feasible; and which policy responses affect output, inflation and distribution. A country issuing its own currency faces a different constraint from one promising foreign currency, but currency issuance still changes real allocations and can alter inflation and future funding costs. The crisis chapter develops these distinctions with explicit balance sheets.

5. Automatic stabilizers and conditional fiscal multipliers

A multiplier measures the output response to a specified fiscal instrument under a specified closure and horizon. Our next experiment has a fixed price level P = 1, slack capacity sufficient for the computed output, no foreign trade or public investment, and a short-run consumption rule. It does not yet describe households' entire lifetime budgets. Let net taxes—taxes less transfers—be N(Y) = T̄ + τY, with 0 ≤ τ ≤ 1. T̄ can be negative. Set

C = c₀ + c[Y − N(Y)],   0 < c < 1,
I = Ī − b(r − r̄),   b ≥ 0,
r = r̄ + ψ(Y − Ȳ),   ψ ≥ 0,
Y = C + I + G.

r is an ordinary real financing rate, and ψ has rate-per-output units. The rate schedule is an explicit local monetary/financial closure; ψ = 0 is a fixed-rate experiment. Expected inflation and risk spreads are held fixed here. Ȳ is a reference level, not an additional market-clearing equation. The government primary surplus in this model is S = N − G. Transfers are already netted in N, so do not subtract them a second time.

D = 1 − c(1 − τ) + bψ > 0,
Y = [c₀ − cT̄ + Ī + bψȲ + G]/D,
∂Y/∂G = 1/D,   ∂Y/∂T̄ = −c/D,   ∂Y/∂Ī = 1/D.

D > 0 follows from c < 1, τ ≥ 0 and bψ ≥ 0; it proves uniqueness of the algebraic solution. Check additionally that C, I and Y are nonnegative, rates remain in the maintained domain, and available capacity can accommodate Y. Future taxes, expectations, supply responses and financial risk can change these reduced-form schedules, so this multiplier is conditional.

Higher τ reduces the response to an autonomous spending disturbance: some income losses automatically lower net taxes, supporting disposable income. This is an automatic stabilizer, operating under unchanged rules. To compare stabilization strength at a common starting point, adjust T̄ so the initial tax burden and equilibrium stay fixed; changing τ without this adjustment mixes a level change with the shock response. Automatic stabilization also makes the observed budget deteriorate during a downturn even without a discretionary expansion.

CBO's August 2026 methodological discussion distinguishes rule-driven budget responses to cyclical conditions from legislative changes. Its estimates condition revenue and selected spending on output and unemployment gaps. A cyclically adjusted balance is consequently a model-based estimate, not direct observation of policy intent; omitted cyclical channels and uncertain potential output matter. We use this methodological distinction only, not the report's projections or dated fiscal amounts.

Worked example 3 — Smoothing a shock, then changing a debt denominator

Set c₀ = 10, c = 3/4, τ = 1/5, T̄ = 0, Ī = 30, G = 40 and ψ = 0. D = 2/5, so Y = 200, N = 40, C = 130 and S = 0. An investment-intercept shock of −8 lowers Y by 20 to 180. Net taxes fall to 36, consumption to 118 and investment to 22; 118 + 22 + 40 = 180. The primary deficit is 4 even though the fiscal rule did not change.

For comparison set τ = 0 and T̄ = 40, keeping the original Y = 200, net taxes 40 and primary balance zero. Now D = 1/4. The same −8 shock lowers output by 32 to 168. Consumption is 106, investment 22 and G 40; the budget stays balanced. Under the maintained schedules, the automatic revenue decline of 4 accompanies a smaller output loss of 20 rather than 32. That is insurance over this short-run disturbance, not a claim that deficits are always beneficial.

Return to the initial τ = 1/5 baseline and consider a separate spending cut of x = 4, with T̄ fixed and investment unchanged. Output falls by (5/2)4 = 10 to 190. Taxes fall to 38; spending is 36; the primary surplus improves by only 2. Suppose, solely for this one-period comparison, opening debt is 160, interest is zero and A = 0. Baseline ending debt is 160; after the cut it is 158. The debt ratio nevertheless rises from 160/200 = 0.8 to 158/190 = 79/95 ≈ 0.831579.

More generally, if the spending multiplier is m and baseline end debt and GDP are B and Y, a small cut x gives d(x) = [B − (1 − τm)x]/[Y − mx], with positive denominator. Its derivative is [mB − Y(1 − τm)]/(Y − mx)². In this case it is positive: 2.5(160) − 200(0.5) = 300. This establishes a possible short-run denominator effect. It does not establish the long-run debt path or welfare effect of an actual consolidation; growth, interest, expectations and the spending's purpose remain consequential.

The fiscal and monetary closures interact. At the same baseline, take b = 100, ψ = 0.002, r̄ = 0.03 and Ȳ = 200. Then bψ = 0.2 and the spending multiplier falls from 2.5 to 5/3. Raising G by 12 raises output by 20, the rate by 0.04 and lowers investment by 4. Consumption rises by 12, so the goods-market change is 12 − 4 + 12 = 20. Both the spending increase and the accompanying rate response belong in the experiment.

A simultaneous equal increase ΔG = ΔT̄ has multiplier (1 − c)/D with respect to that common change. The textbook value one requires additional restrictions, such as τ = 0 and ψ = 0 here. With the worked case's τ = 1/5 and ψ = 0, an increase of 4 in both instruments raises output by 2.5; automatic revenue then adds 0.5 beyond the explicit tax increase. A “balanced budget change” in the chosen instruments need not leave the realized balance unchanged.

6. Financing, household heterogeneity and distribution

A current tax cut may change liquidity without increasing lifetime resources. Consider one price-taking household in a two-date economy with fixed real gross rate R > 0 and unchanged government purchases. Its lifetime consumption budget is C₀ + C₁/R = y₀ − T₀ + (y₁ − T₁)/R. Cut its current lump-sum tax by Δ and raise its own future tax by RΔ. The change in lifetime disposable wealth is Δ − RΔ/R = 0.

With unchanged preferences, the same feasible lifetime set, unrestricted borrowing and saving at R, and credible taxes on the same household, its set of optimal consumption paths is unchanged; when the optimum is unique, the consumption path is unchanged. This is the financing-neutrality benchmark called Ricardian equivalence. It does not say government spending has no resource cost or benefit. Distortionary taxes, credit constraints, different borrowing costs, uncertainty, changing spending, or a future tax burden on different people can invalidate the stated argument. A government's longer horizon than an individual household requires an additional intergenerational link; it cannot simply be assumed away.

Eric Sims's Spring 2026 lecture supplies a primary teaching reference for the two-date budget argument and its borrowing-constraint and tax assumptions. Our household examples are partial-equilibrium experiments with available external counterparties at the given rate. They do not assert that every household in a closed economy can borrow simultaneously without an aggregate financing counterpart.

Worked example 4 — Same lifetime resources, different ability to spend now

Let R = 1 and utility be ln C₀ + ln C₁. Baseline disposable incomes are 20 now and 60 later. With no borrowing constraint the household chooses C₀ = C₁ = 40, borrowing 20. Concavity proves the equal-consumption interior choice is the unique optimum over positive consumption with total resources 80.

A tax reduction of 10 now, financed by an extra tax of 10 on the same household later, changes disposable incomes to 30 and 50. Total resources remain 80. Consumption remains (40, 40); borrowing falls to 10. The tax reduction changes the financial position, not the optimal consumption allocation.

Now prohibit borrowing, while allowing saving. Initially C₀ ≤ 20; the unconstrained optimum is unavailable, so the optimum is (20, 60). After the tax shift C₀ ≤ 30 and the optimum is (30, 50). To verify the boundary, substitute C₁ = 80 − C₀: the utility derivative 1/C₀ − 1/(80 − C₀) is positive for C₀ < 40. The tax shift relaxes a binding liquidity constraint and raises current consumption by 10 despite unchanged lifetime wealth. This is a household response, not an aggregate-output multiplier.

Distribution matters even when aggregate revenue and expenditure match. If a one-time balanced transfer moves 10 from a household with a current marginal propensity to consume of 0.2 to one with propensity 1, the immediate consumption change under those fixed responses is 10 − 2 = 8. This is an impact spending calculation, not a welfare theorem or a complete market equilibrium. Tax incidence, prices, future taxes, labor responses and the value of public services can change the ultimate allocation.

Evaluate a fiscal program by who receives services or insurance, who supplies resources now, who holds the debt, who bears future taxes and risk, and whether the program changes productive capacity. A project with valuable future benefits may increase measured debt initially; a wasteful program can do the same. Accounting alone cannot distinguish them. Likewise, restoring fiscal capacity through a cut to high-value investment may differ from cutting a low-value subsidy even if the first-year deficit reduction is identical.

An empirical multiplier requires a causal design. Policy often responds to forecasts, recessions or disasters, so regressing output changes on budget changes can mix cause and response. Specify the unexpected policy component, announcement and implementation dates, counterfactual, horizon and units. A cumulative output response divided by cumulative additional purchases is a different statistic from a one-period growth coefficient. A narrative policy instrument, randomized local program or institutional discontinuity needs its own exclusion and spillover arguments; none becomes valid merely by being named. Connect these questions to causal identification before presenting a calibrated multiplier as evidence.

Reproducible fiscal-path laboratory

The laboratory instructions, synthetic inputs, standard-library program and benchmark output implement nominal stocks and current-GDP fiscal flows, then reconcile the ratio law independently. They compare a fixed primary surplus, an unconstrained response rule, a capped rule and two stress paths. A cap violation and a terminal present-value residual are reported rather than silently repaired. They are conditional arithmetic, not a sovereign credit score.

Exercises

  1. Three different financing numbers. Opening debt is 150, opening GDP 250, i = 0.06, inflation 0.04 and real growth −0.02. The primary deficit is 5. Government draws down 3 of its opening cash asset of 10 and 30 of principal matures. Compute ending GDP, overall deficit before the cash draw, new issuance, debt change, ending gross debt and gross and specified net-debt ratios. Assume par transactions and no other adjustments. Reconcile the cash draw without counting it as revenue.
  2. An approximation reverses the sign. Let i = 0.08, π = 0.10, g = −0.05, d₀ = 0.75, p = 0.024 and a = 0. Compute the exact ratio change and compare it with (i − π − g)d₀ − p. Express the results in percentage points of GDP. Derive the exact real rate and check the real-rate version of the identity.
  3. Stability versus implementability. Use Worked example 2. Derive the entire interval of φ giving asymptotic stability. If the primary-surplus ratio cannot exceed 0.05, can the φ = 0.25 rule be implemented immediately from d₀ = 0.9? Compute the first ratio under the capped rule. Derive the constant-rate debt threshold under this fiscal cap and explain what it does and does not establish. Separately take α = 1, p = 0.02 and d₀ = 0.8: when does gross debt first reach zero?
  4. Keep the terminal term. With B₀ = 100, R₁ = R₂ = 1.1, A = 0 and S₁ = 20, choose S₂ so B₂ = 0. Verify the present-value equation. Instead set S₂ = 88 and compute the remaining debt and discounted terminal value. Finally verify the chapter's constant-ratio R < Γ counterexample and explain why it does not satisfy the imposed vanishing-terminal condition.
  5. A new automatic stabilizer. Let c₀ = 10, c = 0.8, τ = 0.25, T̄ = 0, Ī = 20, G = 30 and ψ = 0. Solve the baseline, then reduce Ī by 6 with no fiscal-rule change. Report Y, net taxes, C, I and the primary surplus in each case. Compare the output shock with a τ = 0 system whose T̄ is adjusted to preserve the original baseline. Explain what is held fixed.
  6. Instruments and a denominator. Use exercise 5's original baseline. First raise both G and T̄ by 4 and solve the change in output and the primary surplus. Separately set bψ = 0.2 while holding the original baseline fixed, and raise only G by 6: compute output, investment and consumption changes. Finally return to ψ = 0 and cut G by 4; if baseline end debt is 120, the interest bill is fixed and A = 0, compute new end debt and its GDP ratio. Do not extrapolate the last result into a long-run welfare verdict.
  7. Whose future taxes? At R = 1 with utility ln C₀ + ln C₁, a household has disposable incomes (24, 72). A tax cut of 12 now is matched by an extra tax of 12 on the same household later. Find consumption and borrowing before and after with unrestricted credit; repeat when borrowing is forbidden. If the future tax instead falls on someone else, what happens to the recipient's lifetime wealth? Explain why aggregate fiscal balance alone does not establish household neutrality or a welfare ranking.
  8. A decision memo with two paths. Start from B₀ = Z₀ = 100. For three periods Path A has R = 1.03, Γ = 1.05, p = 0.01 and a = 0. Path B has R = 1.07, Γ = 1, p = −0.02, and a = 0.10 in period 1 only. Compute each final stock and ratio, respecting the current-GDP denominators. State what additional information is required for a financing decision and a distributional judgment. Can these two unweighted scenarios identify a default probability or an empirical fiscal multiplier? Propose one concrete identification threat and one useful evidence check.
Complete solutions

  1. Γ = 1.04(0.98) = 1.0192 and Z₁ = 254.8. Interest is 9; S = −5, so the overall deficit is 14. The asset draw makes A = −3. New issuance is 30 + 9 + 5 − 3 = 41; debt increases by 11 to 161. The independent stock calculation is 150 − 30 + 41 = 161. Gross debt/GDP is 161/254.8 = 805/1274 ≈ 0.631868. Cash ends at 7, giving the specified net debt 154 and ratio 770/1274 = 385/637 ≈ 0.604396. Opening net debt was 140, so net debt rises by the full deficit of 14. Treating the cash draw as revenue would confuse a financing source with the primary balance and obscure this reconciliation.

  2. Γ = 1.045, α = 1.08/1.045 = 216/209 and α − 1 = 7/209. Thus Δd = (7/209)(3/4) − 3/125 = 117/104500 ≈ 0.001119617: an increase of about 0.111962 percentage points. The approximate expression is (0.08 − 0.10 + 0.05)0.75 − 0.024 = −0.0015, a decline of 0.15 percentage points. Omitting the interaction and denominator reverses the direction here.

    The real rate is 1.08/1.10 − 1 = −1/55. Therefore (r − g)/(1 + g) = (−1/55 + 1/20)/(19/20) = 7/209, reproducing the exact change. Inflation and growth are sufficiently large that the first-order shortcut is misleading for this small net debt-ratio change.

  3. |1.05 − φ| < 1 gives 0.05 < φ < 2.05. At either endpoint the deviation does not decay. From 0.9 the requested surplus is 0.04 + 0.25(0.1) = 0.065, above the cap. Capping it at 0.05 instead gives d₁ = 1.05(0.9) − 0.05 = 0.895. The unconstrained linear convergence formula cannot be used for that step.

    The threshold is 0.05/(1.05 − 1) = 1. Above 1, even the permanent maximum surplus produces a growing deviation from 1; at 1 it holds the ratio, and below 1 it reduces debt. Thus the failure to implement this particular feedback rule at 0.9 does not establish that all adjustment paths fail: the capped first step already lowers debt. The threshold assumes fixed rates and growth, no adjustments, and a feasible permanent cap; it is not a universal default boundary. With α = 1, dₜ = 0.8 − 0.02t, first reaching zero at t = 40. Stop the gross-debt rule there or specify how further surpluses build assets.

  4. B₁ = 110 − 20 = 90, so S₂ must be 99. Then 20/1.1 + 99/1.21 = 200/11 + 900/11 = 100. With S₂ = 88, B₂ = 11. Discounted primary surpluses sum to 1000/11 ≈ 90.9091; discounted terminal debt is 11/1.21 = 100/11 ≈ 9.0909. Their sum still equals 100. Deleting the terminal term would incorrectly report a satisfied terminal repayment condition.

    In the constant-ratio counterexample, α = 34/35 and p = −4/175 yield α(4/5) − p = 4/5. However, discounted nominal debt grows with (35/34)ᵗ. A bounded ratio has therefore not supplied the vanishing discounted terminal value. This diagnoses failure of that specific terminal restriction; a different equilibrium model requires its own justified financing and terminal assumptions.

  5. D = 1 − 0.8(0.75) = 0.4, so baseline Y = 60/0.4 = 150. Net taxes are 37.5, consumption is 10 + 0.8(112.5) = 100, investment 20 and the primary surplus 7.5. After the investment shock, Y = 54/0.4 = 135, N = 33.75, C = 91, I = 14 and S = 3.75. Goods clear: 91 + 14 + 30 = 135. The primary surplus falls by 3.75 automatically.

    For τ = 0 choose T̄ = 37.5 to preserve the baseline tax burden. The numerator is then 10 − 0.8(37.5) + 20 + 30 = 30 and D = 0.2, again giving 150. The −6 shock lowers output by 30 to 120, with N = 37.5, C = 76, I = 14 and S = 7.5. Initial output, revenue, spending and private schedules at the baseline are held fixed; the different tax response to income drives the different shock sensitivity.

  6. Equal instrument changes give ΔY = [(1 − 0.8)/0.4]4 = 2. Net taxes rise by 4 + 0.25(2) = 4.5; spending rises by 4, so the primary surplus rises by 0.5 to 8. It is not unchanged. With rate feedback bψ = 0.2 and the reference/intercept chosen to preserve the baseline, D = 0.6. A purchases increase of 6 raises output by 10; investment changes by −0.2(10) = −2 and consumption by 0.8(1 − 0.25)10 = 6. Goods-market changes sum to 6 − 2 + 6 = 10.

    Separately, without rate feedback the cut of 4 lowers output by 10 to 140. Net taxes fall by 2.5; the primary surplus rises by 1.5 to 9. With the interest bill and other financing flows unchanged, debt falls from 120 to 118.5. Its ratio rises from 0.8 to 118.5/140 = 237/280 ≈ 0.846429. A smaller nominal numerator does not ensure a smaller ratio when GDP contracts. The horizon is one period; future financing, productive effects, expectations and distribution are not resolved by this calculation.

  7. Total lifetime disposable resources are 96. Under unrestricted credit the unique log-utility optimum is (48, 48). Before the tax shift the household borrows 24; after disposable incomes become (36, 60), it borrows 12. With borrowing forbidden, current consumption is at its upper bound: (24, 72) before and (36, 60) after. The derivative 1/C₀ − 1/(96 − C₀) is positive below 48, so these binding-bound choices are optimal.

    If someone else pays the future tax, the recipient gains 12 of lifetime disposable wealth at R = 1; the future payer loses 12, before behavioral or price effects. Aggregate present-value balance does not cancel each individual's tax change. Welfare comparisons require preferences, initial resources, incidence and social weights or a stated efficiency criterion. A claim of neutrality must match the tax payer, timing, borrowing access and spending path; merely adding government taxes and debt is insufficient.

  8. Path A has GDP 105, 110.25 and 115.7625. Current surpluses are 1.05, 1.1025 and 1.157625. Debt is 101.95, 103.906 and 105.865555, so final d = 105.865555/115.7625 ≈ 0.914506. Path B has GDP 100 throughout. Its primary balance is −2 per period and the first adjustment is 10. Debt is 119, 129.33 and 140.3831; final d = 1.403831. The first-period B increase is 7 interest + 2 primary deficit + 10 adjustment. The adjustment must be named—such as an asset acquisition at the stated valuation—before interpreting its welfare or net-debt effect.

    A financing memo needs maturity dates, cash and saleable assets, currency, refinancing capacity, interest repricing, contingent liabilities and feasible fiscal responses. A distributional memo names affected taxpayers, service recipients, workers and creditors, and asks whether spending changes future productive capacity. No probabilities accompany these paths; their frequency cannot be inferred. No observed exogenous policy variation identifies a multiplier here. One concrete threat is discretionary spending rising in response to private forecasts of a downturn. A useful evidence check matches decision and announcement dates to information available then, separates forecast-driven changes from the proposed policy shock, and examines pre-policy output paths; that check helps assess, but alone does not prove, an exclusion restriction. Grade for correct accounts, explicit missing information and a concrete threat/check pair, not for choosing a predetermined policy.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back: explain why a government can have a primary surplus, issue many new bonds and still face a funding crisis. Derive the ratio law from the nominal budget, identify current versus prior GDP, then explain why a fixed-point surplus is not necessarily a stable fiscal rule. Finish with one household for whom a tax shift is neutral and one for whom it changes current consumption.

Teach-back checklist

A complete answer separates interest, maturing principal and asset transactions from the primary balance; compares new issuance with refinancing capacity; derives α = (1 + i)/[(1 + π)(1 + g)]; and states the deviation factor α − φ for a feedback rule. It keeps solvency conditional on resources and terminal assumptions distinct from access to cash today. The financing-neutral household can smooth freely and bears the same present-value taxes; a constrained household's current feasible set changes. Neither the ratio identity nor a short-run multiplier independently establishes a welfare ranking.

Delayed check: with R = Γ = 1.04, d₀ = 0.6, p = 0.015 and a = 0.005, find next debt/GDP. If 20% of opening debt matures, is new issuance just the debt-stock change? For c = 0.6, τ = 0.25 and bψ = 0.05, derive the purchases multiplier and the equal-tax-and-purchases multiplier. State one reason an observed budget deterioration need not imply discretionary stimulus.

Delayed-check answer

α = 1 and d₁ = 0.59. When A represents cash flows, new issuance equals maturing principal plus the debt-stock change, not the change alone; convert the ratio figures to nominal stocks using GDP before computing its amount. Here D = 1 − 0.6(0.75) + 0.05 = 0.6, giving a purchases multiplier 5/3 and an equal-instrument multiplier (0.4)/(0.6) = 2/3. Lower income can automatically reduce net taxes under unchanged legislation; a cyclical adjustment additionally depends on an estimated counterfactual and may omit relevant channels.

Further study and connection

This chapter establishes accounting identities and bounded models; it does not solve the full optimal-tax problem or estimate country-specific fiscal capacity. Graduate extensions require distortionary taxation, incomplete insurance, sovereign default incentives, stochastic discount factors and fiscal–monetary equilibrium selection. The next chapter, Trade and comparative advantage, studies international allocation and distribution; subsequent external-account and crisis chapters add foreign-currency valuation and refinancing constraints. Preserve the distinction between a model's feasible path, evidence for its parameters and a defensible policy decision.

Sources and further study

  • Julio Escolano — A Practical Guide to Public Debt Dynamics, Fiscal Sustainability, and Cyclical Adjustment of Budgetary Aggregates (IMF Technical Notes and Manuals 10/02, January 2010) — Exact debt/GDP accounting and the distinction between constant ratios, stability and explicit terminal financing restrictions; no historical estimates imported.
  • Congressional Budget Office — Effects of Automatic Stabilizers on the Federal Budget: 2026 to 2036 (August 2026) — Methodological distinction between automatic budget responses and discretionary fiscal action, and limitations of cyclical adjustment; no projection figures used.
  • Eric Sims, University of Notre Dame — Lecture 11: Debt, Taxes, and Ricardian Equivalence, ECON 30020 (Spring 2026) — Primary two-date teaching reference for household and government PV budgets and conditional financing neutrality.
